title: Braille & Seeing Without Sight
description: Umbra's final trick plunges the world into darkness. But the greatest lesson of all: people who cannot see still read, learn and thrive. Master it to restore the Rainbow Crystal!

content.value: People who are visually impaired can read and write using BRAILLE — a system of raised dots felt with the fingertips. It was developed by Louis Braille, who was himself blind, in the 1820s.

Braille uses a 'cell' of up to six raised dots, arranged in two columns of three. Different patterns of raised dots stand for different letters, numbers and even musical notes. By moving their fingers across the dots, a reader recognises each pattern quickly.

A Braille cell = 6 dot positions
  1 • • 4
  2 • • 5
  3 • • 6
Raising different dots makes different letters:
  A = dot 1     B = dots 1,2     C = dots 1,4

Beyond Braille, many aids help people with limited vision live fully: walking canes, guide dogs, audiobooks, screen-reader software that speaks text aloud, and Braille keyboards and displays for computers. Technology keeps opening new doors.

Being visually impaired does not stop people from achieving great things — many scientists, musicians, teachers and athletes are blind or partially sighted. Other senses, like touch and hearing, often become remarkably sharp.

Key Takeaway: Braille is a touch-based system of raised dots that lets visually impaired people read and write. Along with canes, audiobooks and screen readers, it helps everyone access knowledge — with or without sight.

quiz.question: Braille is read by…
options: feeling patterns of raised dots with the fingertips
quiz.explain: Braille uses raised dots that a reader feels with their fingertips to recognise letters and numbers.

quiz.question: How many dot positions are in a single standard Braille cell?
quiz.explain: A Braille cell has six dot positions, in two columns of three. Different raised patterns make different characters.

quiz.question: Which of these is an aid for people with limited vision?
options: A screen reader that speaks text aloud
quiz.explain: Screen readers, audiobooks, canes and guide dogs all help visually impaired people access information and move safely.
